A branch current sensor measures total current upstream of the connector contactors. A controller communicates with the connector interfaces and contactors over an isolated local bus.

It first assigns the minimum sustaining current to sessions that can receive it, then distributes remaining current according to energy deficit. The controller sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface and verifies the resulting connector current with the corresponding current sensor.

The branch current sensor is an independent safety input. If measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command for a verification interval, the controller opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit. A contactor is not reclosed until its connector current sensor reports zero, the control-pilot interface reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired. A welded-contactor condition is recorded when connector current remains above a leakage threshold after an open command. The controller then inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates a local fault indicator.

The controller can receive remote schedules and authorizations through a network interface, but it stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. During a network outage it continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process. It does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.

A service input permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the corresponding connector current sensor. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. This prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

The disclosed essential relationship is closed-loop allocation using both per-connector current sensing and independent upstream branch sensing, with staged reduction followed by ordered contactor shedding when branch current does not respond. Offline authorization, welded-contactor isolation, tamper-evident records, and installation mapping are supported additional features.

content.content:
1	Sites that install several electric-vehicle charging connectors frequently supply those connectors from a single electrical branch. The branch is protected at an allowable aggregate current, referred to herein as a branch limit, that is commonly lower than the sum of the individual connector ratings. Installing a branch large enough for every connector to draw its full rating at the same time is often impractical, because the cost of the additional service capacity, conductors, and protective devices can exceed the cost of the charging equipment itself.
2	
3	Charging equipment therefore has to share a fixed amount of current among connectors that could collectively demand more. The signalling mechanism ordinarily available for that purpose is the control pilot presented to each vehicle, which advertises a maximum current that the vehicle is permitted to draw. Control-pilot signalling is advisory in nature. The value advertised on the pilot is a command, not a measurement, and the current actually drawn depends on the behaviour of the vehicle receiving it. A vehicle may respond slowly, may respond only in coarse steps, may hold a previous value while its own thermal or state-of-charge logic settles, or may not reduce at all. Control that assumes the commanded value is the delivered value therefore has no way to detect the case in which the branch remains loaded above its limit after a reduction has been ordered, and that case is precisely the one in which the branch protective device is at risk of operating and removing service from every connector on the branch.
4	
5	A further difficulty arises because the branch usually carries loads other than charging. Lighting, building services, and other equipment on the same branch consume part of the allowable aggregate current, and that consumption varies through the day. Allocation that divides the full branch limit among the connectors, without accounting for the varying non-charging portion of the branch load, either overcommits the branch or forces the installer to configure a permanently conservative limit that wastes capacity for most of the day.
6	
7	Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.
8	
9	Charging equipment is additionally exposed to conditions that are specific to its power path and its installation. A contactor whose contacts have welded continues to pass current after an open command has been issued, so an allocation scheme that treats an open command as removal of the load will continue to believe that capacity has been released when it has not. Site communication to a remote management system is not continuous, so equipment that depends on a remote authority for both authorization and current limits either stops serving vehicles when the link fails or continues without a governing limit. Multi-connector equipment is also wired by hand, and a transposition between the logical identifier of a connector and the physical contactor and sensor channel that serve it causes a current limit intended for one connector to be applied to another, which defeats the allocation entirely while leaving every individual component apparently functional.
10	
11	There remains a need for charging control that treats the current actually present on the branch and at each connector as the governing quantity, that keeps the branch within its limit even when a vehicle does not honour a reduced pilot command, that allocates the genuinely available portion of the branch limit in a way that corrects accumulated inequality between sessions, and that remains safe and operable when the site link is down, when a contactor has welded, and when the installation wiring map has not been independently confirmed.
12

3	Overview of the system
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.
6	
7	The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.
8	
9	A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.
10	
11	The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.
12	
13	A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.
14	
15	The connector station
16
